transcript:
Meeting header: Date: 2026-04-18T15:00:00Z
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Laura Chen (Redwood AE); Marcus Diaz (Redwood SE); Sana Patel (DataHarbor - Head of ML); Mark O'Neill (DataHarbor - Infra Eng); Priya Rao (DataHarbor - Product); Luis Gomez (SRE)

Summary: POC will scope integrating DataHarbor's customer load scripts into Redwood's benchmark harness to run streaming and non-streaming load tests. Success criteria: latency p50/p95/p99 targets, throughput (reqs/sec and tokens/sec), cost per million tokens, and functional correctness (no hallucination/regressions). Timeline: baseline run then optimization window, final results and recommendations.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Laura Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out the time. Quick intro, I'm Laura, I'll be your AE and coordinating the pilot. Marcus is our SE who will own the harness integration.
[00:18] Marcus Diaz: Hi all, hey, hi — Marcus here. I'll walk through the harness, examples we have, and what we need from you to run meaningful benchmarks.
[00:30] Sana Patel: Thanks, Laura. We're excited. High level, our main goals: (1) confirm latency/throughput on real workloads, (2) validate streaming end-to-end for our chat UI, and (3) get an apples-to-apples cost estimate vs our on-prem cluster.
[00:46] Laura Chen: Great, that's exactly what we wanted to cover. Before we dive — what does your current stack look like for inference?
[00:54] Mark O'Neill: We run an internal GPU pool, mixed P40/V100s and some custom scaling. We use an in-house routing layer; most of our traffic is non-streaming RPC for batch summarization, but the chat product is token-streaming.
[01:10] Marcus Diaz: Okay. So we should benchmark both streaming and non-streaming profiles separately — they stress different parts of the runtime (batching, KV cache, continuous decoding).
[01:23] Sana Patel: Correct. For chat we care about tail latency — p95/p99 under 250ms ideally. For batch jobs we care about throughput and cost per 1M tokens.
[01:36] Laura Chen: Noted. On the POC scope: we usually do a baseline run using the harness with your scripts to reproduce production-like traffic, then tune batching, quantization, and caching for a second run. Typical POC timeline is two weeks, with an optional week three for deeper perf tuning. Is that workable?
[01:54] Priya Rao: Two weeks sounds ok. We do need security sign-off though — we need your security checklist and SOC/ISO docs.
[02:03] Laura Chen: We'll share the security pack in the next 24 hours. Marcus will share the harness and a small example repo.
[02:11] Marcus Diaz: Quick note on the harness: it's a small repo with adapters for k6 and Locust and a python runner we call 'redwood-bench'. It accepts scripted input (your query files), concurrency profile, and streaming vs non-streaming flag. We have Docker images if you want to run locally or we can run it from our dedicated cluster.
[02:33] Mark O'Neill: We prefer to run our scripts on your dedicated cluster to avoid differences in our infra, but we need a VPC peering option or an agent. How do you handle network isolation?
[02:44] Marcus Diaz: For Private/Pilot we can do VPC peering or a temporary tunnelling agent; for hosted we run in our environment. For this POC we suggest running the harness against a Redwood dedicated test instance in a sandbox VPC. We'll provide connection details and an ephemeral key.
[02:59] Sana Patel: Sounds good. On the workload side, we'll provide: (a) 1k chat transcripts for streaming tests, (b) 2k batch summarization scripts, and (c) a target concurrency map (normal + 2x spike). We also have some pre-processing steps — small tokens normalization — we'll share the exact steps.
[03:20] Marcus Diaz: Perfect. For the streaming harness we measure time-to-first-token, steady-state tokens/sec, and p95/p99 for response completion. For non-streaming we measure end-to-end latency and throughput. The harness will generate reports: latency histograms, tokens/sec, CPU/GPU utilization if you attach metrics, and a cost estimate (based on token counts and our runtime profile).
[03:41] Priya Rao: How do you estimate cost though? We need comparable metrics to our on-prem $/1M tokens.
[03:47] Laura Chen: We compute cost from observed tokens/sec, average GPU utilization and our published price curves for the selected model/instance. We'll send an exported report that includes assumptions and line-item costs.
[03:58] Sana Patel: Important: we will also want to replicate the runs with quantized model variants (8-bit) to see the cost/latency tradeoffs. Does the harness support switching model profiles?
[04:08] Marcus Diaz: Yes — the harness accepts a model profile parameter. We include three model variants: full fp16, int8-quantized, and a lower-capacity model for fallback. We also support KV cache warm starts to simulate repeated prefixes.
[04:22] Mark O'Neill: Do you have any sample scripts for KV cache warm-up? Our traffic is heavy on repeated contexts so cache behavior matters a lot.
[04:30] Marcus Diaz: We do. I'll include a 'prefix-warm' scenario that replays top 50 prefixes to warm the KV cache. Just note sometimes the transcriber (uh, the docs) writes K-V cash — so, K-V cache — but it's the same thing.
[04:44] Sana Patel: (laughs) helpful. On measurement windows: we want a baseline 4-hour run with steady-state traffic and a 30-minute spike to validate autoscaling. Is that in scope?
[04:55] Marcus Diaz: Yes, that's fine. For autoscaling we can simulate spike with a step-load profile. If you want autoscaling tests, we need to nail expected metrics — e.g., scale threshold at 70% GPU util or queue length.
[05:10] Laura Chen: Also want to confirm success criteria — Sana, can you read out what would make this POC a win for you?
[05:18] Sana Patel: Sure: (1) streaming p95 < 250ms for our median chat prompt, (2) non-streaming throughput at least 2x our current on-prem per-GPU token throughput, or cost improvement of >=25% per 1M tokens, (3) no functional regressions on our eval prompts (QA pass), and (4) integration friction low — documented steps to plug in harness.
[05:36] Laura Chen: Great. We'll aim to produce a results deck that maps directly to those criteria.
[05:41] Priya Rao: One question on data: when you run the harness in your sandbox, do logs or transcripts leave our control? We need retention guarantees.
[05:50] Laura Chen: We can run under an isolated tenant and redact logs on request. We'll include the retention and access controls in the security docs.
[05:58] Mark O'Neill: For the actual execution, what's the minimum we need to provide? Just input scripts and concurrency map?
[06:04] Marcus Diaz: That's the minimum. Also a small eval set for correctness checks and an example request/response schema so the harness can validate outputs. If you have promp templates or few-shot contexts included, include those too.
[06:17] Sana Patel: We'll include a few-shot variant — sometimes we see latency differences when context window grows.
[06:23] Marcus Diaz: Good call. We'll parameterize sequence length in the harness so you can run short and long context tests.
[06:30] Laura Chen: Logistics and timeline recap: Marcus shares harness + examples by 2026-04-20; Sana uploads scripts by 2026-04-22; Mark shares concurrency profile by 2026-04-19. Kickoff run scheduled for week of 2026-04-27 with a baseline and spike window. Final report and recommendations by week of 2026-05-04. Any blockers?
[06:50] Mark O'Neill: Security review timeline might be a blocker — we need our security team to review the docs. How long does that usually take?
[06:57] Laura Chen: For pilot customers it's usually 3-5 business days once they have the security pack. We can do a 1:1 with your security reviewer if needed.
[07:06] Luis Gomez: (joined) Sorry, late. Quick Q: do you instrument GPU-level metrics? We want to map utilization to tokens/sec.
[07:13] Marcus Diaz: Yes, we collect GPU utilization, memory, and per-process metrics; if you provide a Prometheus endpoint we can ingest it or we can push CSVs.
[07:22] Sana Patel: Another question — when you run streaming tests, do you simulate network conditions (latency/jitter)? We have some mobile users with poor networks.
[07:31] Marcus Diaz: We have options in the harness to throttle network or add latency in the client runner. But for infra-level latency we measure server-side times; we can run both to separate concerns.
[07:42] Priya Rao: That sounds comprehensive. One last ask: can the harness produce a consolidated CSV with p50/p95/p99 for both streaming (time-to-first-token and completion) and non-streaming?
[07:52] Marcus Diaz: Yes, that's standard output.
[07:55] Laura Chen: Ok, wrapping up — recap of next steps and owners: Marcus will share harness and example scripts (k6/Locust + redwood-bench) by 2026-04-20; Laura will send SOW and security pack by 2026-04-21; Sana will upload scripts and sample records by 2026-04-22; Mark will share concurrency profile by 2026-04-19; schedule baseline run week of 2026-04-27.
[08:18] Sana Patel: Thanks. Can you also include a short how-to for model profile switches (fp16 vs int8) so our ML folks can understand tradeoffs?
[08:26] Marcus Diaz: Yep, included. I'll add a short doc and a couple of example commands.
[08:31] Laura Chen: Perfect. If no other Qs we'll close. We'll follow up in email with links. Thanks everyone.
[08:38] Priya Rao: Thanks all.
[08:40] Mark O'Neill: Thanks.
[08:42] Luis Gomez: Thanks.

End of transcript.

Notes about transcription quality: medium — some speaker labels and proper nouns may be off; occasional transcription artifacts (e.g., "K-V cash" instead of "KV cache").

Referenced artifacts/links: Redwood benchmark harness repo (link shared in chat), security pack (sent after call), example k6/Locust scripts (attached).

POC success criteria (recap): streaming p95 < 250ms; non-streaming throughput >= 2x per-GPU or >=25% cost savings per 1M tokens; QA pass on eval prompts; documented harness integration steps.

End.
